summary:
Hothis Groot Gardener is a space gardening simulator designed to help astronauts practice crop management decisions during long-duration space missions.

Growing fresh vegetables in space can support astronauts' physical health by supplementing stored food, which loses nutrients over time. Plant care may also benefit psychological well-being. However, problems such as water shortages, excessive moisture, and mold can threaten crop growth and require timely decisions.

Our team developed a simulator based on NASA's Veggie system, where users cultivate 'Outredgeous' red romaine lettuce over seven simulated days representing 33 cultivation days. Users monitor plant health and environmental conditions, adjust watering, lighting, and ventilation, and respond to unexpected problems.

The simulator uses NASA research and actual ISS cultivation cases to evaluate decisions and provide supporting evidence. AI can generate crisis scenarios, while predefined rules determine outcomes to ensure consistent feedback.

By practicing these decisions in a simulated environment, astronauts can become better prepared to recognize crop problems and respond independently during future space missions.
details:
Space Garden Simulator — Hothis Groot Gardener

Project Overview

Space Garden Simulator is an interactive web-based simulation designed to help users understand the challenges of growing vegetables in space. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, the project focuses on cultivating Outredgeous red romaine lettuce in a simulated International Space Station (ISS) Veggie plant growth system.

Astronauts on long-duration space missions depend heavily on stored food, making sustainable food production an important research area. Growing fresh vegetables in space could help supplement astronauts' diets and support their well-being. However, maintaining healthy crops in microgravity presents challenges, including water management, airflow control, and microbial contamination.

Our project allows users to experience these challenges by making cultivation decisions based on real NASA plant growth experiments.

How the Project Works

The simulation represents a 33-day lettuce cultivation period through seven interactive game days.

Users monitor plant health, root moisture, chamber humidity, fan operation, and lighting conditions. They can adjust watering, airflow, and lighting while observing how the simulated environment changes over time.

During cultivation, users encounter crisis scenarios based on problems documented in NASA experiments, including insufficient water supply and excessive moisture combined with poor airflow, which can contribute to mold development.

When a crisis occurs, the system presents the plant's symptoms and several possible actions. Users select an action, and the simulation evaluates their decision using predefined rules supported by scientific research. Their choices affect plant conditions and subsequent gameplay.

At each stage, the system provides a report explaining the outcomes of the user's decisions, along with the scientific evidence and supporting reference materials behind those results. This allows users to understand how their actions affect plant growth and examine the scientific reasoning behind each outcome.

At the end of the mission, users harvest the lettuce, complete sample-handling procedures, and review a final report comparing their simulation results with actual measurements from lettuce grown aboard the ISS.

AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation

The project integrates a Large Language Model (LLM) and an optional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system to provide research-grounded, interactive scenarios.

Our RAG database contains 81 text chunks extracted from scientific research materials related to space-based plant cultivation. A Python-based FastAPI retrieval server uses BM25 keyword search to retrieve four relevant passages and provide them as additional context for the LLM.

For text generation, we use Google's Gemma 4 E4B model running locally through Ollama. The model generates crisis descriptions, dialogue from the lettuce character, symptom clues, action descriptions, and responses to the user's choices. It also supports Korean translation.

An important design decision was to separate AI-generated narration from game logic. The LLM does not determine which action is correct, calculate plant health changes, or generate scientific evidence. These decisions are handled by the simulation engine and a verified evidence database.

To reduce incorrect or misleading AI-generated content, we implemented structured JSON outputs, validation rules, automatic revision attempts, and fallback scenarios. If generated text fails validation, the system uses prewritten content without interrupting gameplay.

During development, we repeatedly tested the generated scenarios and refined the validation process. In the final documented test, all six crisis generations passed validation on their first attempt, with an average generation time of 12.0 seconds in English.

Technologies and Tools

The project uses the following technologies:

  • Frontend and simulation: Next.js, React, TypeScript, HTML, and CSS
  • Backend and AI integration: Python, FastAPI, and server-side TypeScript
  • Language model: Google Gemma 4 E4B, operated locally through Ollama
  • Information retrieval: BM25, ChromaDB, and research-based RAG data
  • Data management: JSON-based scientific evidence, game rules, and simulation records
  • Development tools: Node.js, npm, Git, GitHub, and Claude Code
  • Hardware: A local development laptop capable of running the language model, with GPU acceleration recommended

The simulation can also operate without an active LLM server, allowing users to complete the experience using prewritten scenarios.

Creativity and Innovation

One distinctive feature of Space Garden Simulator is its combination of scientific evidence, interactive decision-making, and a conversational plant character.

Instead of presenting research findings as static information, the project turns documented cultivation problems into situations that users must respond to. The lettuce character communicates symptoms and reactions, making technical plant management concepts easier to engage with.

Another important feature is the separation of generative AI and evidence-based decision-making. Scientific references and predefined simulation rules determine the consequences of user actions, while AI makes the experience more interactive through natural-language generation.

The team also distinguished between values recorded in NASA research and numerical values designed for gameplay. This prevents simulated plant health changes from being presented as actual scientific measurements.

Expected Impact

Space Garden Simulator helps crew members practice crop care decisions for long-duration missions. It can also help the public understand the challenges of producing fresh food in space.

Although the project does not directly measure astronauts' health, it addresses an important condition for supporting their health: maintaining a reliable source of fresh vegetables in space.

By experiencing how water shortages, excessive moisture, and airflow problems affect crop cultivation, users can better understand why environmental monitoring and appropriate intervention matter in space agriculture.

The project also demonstrates how scientific research, rule-based simulation, and generative AI can be combined to create an accessible educational experience.

Our goal is to make space agriculture research easier to understand while encouraging interest in sustainable food production and the technologies needed to support future human space exploration.
